title: Strong diamond property for elementary hammock reductions
statement: Let $P$ be a small ordinary category, let $T\subseteq P$ be a wide subcategory containing identities and closed under composition, let $x,y\in P$, and let $q\geq0$. Use the fixed-word diagrams of [def-coef-zigzag-homotopy-calculus], with only the letters $+,-$. An unreduced hammock is a finite commutative rectangular diagram with $q+1$ rows from $x$ to $y$, all vertical arrows pointing down and lying in $T$, identity vertical arrows at the endpoints, a uniform horizontal direction in each column, and all leftward arrows in $T$. A length-zero diagram exists precisely when $x=y$ and has only identity vertical arrows. No alternation or nonidentity condition is imposed. Define $D\rightsquigarrow D'$ to mean one of the following operations on such diagrams: delete one column all of whose horizontal arrows are identities, identifying its two equal vertex columns and retaining their vertical arrows; or replace two adjacent columns of the same direction by their rowwise composites, deleting the intervening vertex column and retaining all other vertical arrows. These operations produce unreduced hammocks with the same $P,T,x,y,q$. If $D\rightsquigarrow D_1$ and $D\rightsquigarrow D_2$, then either $D_1=D_2$, or there is an unreduced hammock $E$ with $D_1\rightsquigarrow E$ and $D_2\rightsquigarrow E$. Equality here includes the signed word, all vertex objects, and all horizontal and vertical arrows.

source.place: Dwyer–Kan, Calculating simplicial localizations, Definition 2.1, printed p.19, reductions (iv)′ and (v)′; local overlap lemma implicit in Proposition 5.5, printed p.24. Agent formulation and overlap verification; no Stacks tag states this diagram-specific lemma.

proof.text: Number the horizontal columns $1,\ldots,l$ and the vertex columns $0,\ldots,l$. Write $X_i^r$ for the object in row $r$ and vertex column $i$, and $v_i^r:X_i^r\to X_i^{r+1}$ for a vertical arrow. The fixed-word convention of [def-coef-zigzag-homotopy-calculus] identifies an unreduced hammock with its signed word and these objects and arrows satisfying the stated square equations. Use the identity and associative composition laws of [def-nagata-category]. The support of a deletion is its single horizontal column; the support of a composition is its two adjacent horizontal columns. Thus each reduction has a support of size one or two. At length zero neither operation is available; at length one only identity deletion is available.

source.place: Definition 2.1, printed p.19, operations (iv)′ and (v)′; explicit elementary verification of their local overlaps, written by Q02, for Proposition 5.5, printed p.24

proof.text: Check that identity deletion is defined on all the data. If column $i$ consists of identities, then $X_{i-1}^r=X_i^r$ for every row. Its square equation, for either sign, simplifies by the identity laws of [def-nagata-category] to $v_{i-1}^r=v_i^r$. Hence identifying these vertex columns is independent of which copy is retained, including every vertical arrow. The neighbouring squares are unchanged after this equality substitution. Every retained leftward or vertical arrow remains in $T$. Endpoints are preserved; if an endpoint column is identified with its neighbour, the retained vertical arrow equals the original endpoint identity. If deleting the only column gives length zero, all row endpoints coincide, so $x=y$, and all remaining vertical arrows are endpoint identities.

source.place: Definition 2.1, printed p.19, operations (iv)′ and (v)′; explicit elementary verification of their local overlaps, written by Q02, for Proposition 5.5, printed p.24

proof.text:
Check the other operation using [def-nagata-category]. For two rightward columns let their row arrows be $a_r:X_{i-1}^r\to X_i^r$ and $b_r:X_i^r\to X_{i+1}^r$. Their square equations give
$$v_{i+1}^r\circ(b_r\circ a_r)=(b_{r+1}\circ v_i^r)\circ a_r=(b_{r+1}\circ a_{r+1})\circ v_{i-1}^r.$$
For two leftward columns write $a_r:X_i^r\to X_{i-1}^r$ and $b_r:X_{i+1}^r\to X_i^r$. Then
$$v_{i-1}^r\circ(a_r\circ b_r)=(a_{r+1}\circ v_i^r)\circ b_r=(a_{r+1}\circ b_{r+1})\circ v_{i+1}^r.$$
Thus the composite squares commute. The leftward composites lie in $T$ by its assumed closure under composition. All retained objects and vertical arrows, including endpoint identities, are unchanged. There is no requirement to remove a composite that happens to be an identity. These equations verify admissibility in every adjacent pair of rows; for $q=0$ there are no such equations to check.

source.place: Definition 2.1, printed p.19, operations (iv)′ and (v)′; explicit elementary verification of their local overlaps, written by Q02, for Proposition 5.5, printed p.24

proof.text: Suppose the two reductions have exactly the same support and type. They either delete the same identity column or compose the same adjacent pair. The signed words then agree, and the surviving data agree: deletion is unambiguous by step 2, and composition uses the same row composites and retains the same outer vertex columns by step 3. Consequently $D_1=D_2$. No commutativity of morphism composition is being asserted.

source.place: Definition 2.1, printed p.19, operations (iv)′ and (v)′; explicit elementary verification of their local overlaps, written by Q02, for Proposition 5.5, printed p.24

proof.text: Suppose the supports are disjoint, and order them from left to right. Perform both prescribed operations, shifting the position of the right-hand operation down by one after performing the left-hand operation. Each remains available after the other: the other support's horizontal arrows and signs are unchanged. If the supports touch at a vertex, a composition retains that boundary vertex, and a deletion replaces it only by its equal copy with equal vertical arrows as checked in step 2. Two distinct identity deletions therefore remain possible even when adjacent and oppositely signed. In either order the final word replaces each of the two original support blocks by its same shortened word. Objects and vertical arrows outside those blocks are untouched; at a deleted identity boundary they agree by step 2; each composite horizontal arrow is the same row composite on its original block. Hence both orders give literally the same hammock $E$. Each branch reaches it by exactly one permitted reduction. If no horizontal column remains, step 2 verifies the length-zero convention.

source.place: Definition 2.1, printed p.19, operations (iv)′ and (v)′; explicit elementary verification of their local overlaps, written by Q02, for Proposition 5.5, printed p.24

proof.text: Suppose a deletion and a composition have overlapping supports. The identity column being deleted is one of the two columns being composed, and the two signs agree. In every row the composite is the other arrow, since the identity laws of [def-nagata-category] give $a\circ1=a$ and $1\circ a=a$; these are the two possible placements for either sign. Both operations replace that two-column block by the sign and row arrows of the other column. Deletion retains the other column's two vertex columns, whereas composition retains the two outer vertex columns. The only possible difference is one vertex column across the identity column; step 2 identifies its objects and vertical arrows exactly. All data outside the block are unchanged. Therefore $D_1=D_2$, also when both columns consist of identities.

source.place: Definition 2.1, printed p.19, operations (iv)′ and (v)′; explicit elementary verification of their local overlaps, written by Q02, for Proposition 5.5, printed p.24

proof.text: It remains to consider distinct overlapping compositions. Their supports must be $\{i,i+1\}$ and $\{i+1,i+2\}$. Both pairs being composable in the reduction sense forces all three signs to agree. After either first composition, compose the resulting column with the remaining column of this triple, one further permitted reduction. For rightward row arrows $a,b,c$ the two resulting arrows are $c\circ(b\circ a)$ and $(c\circ b)\circ a$. For leftward row arrows $a,b,c$, listed in spatial order, they are $(a\circ b)\circ c$ and $a\circ(b\circ c)$. Each pair is equal by associativity in [def-nagata-category]. In both branches the final word has one column of the common sign in place of the triple. Both delete the same two internal vertex columns, retain the same two outer vertex columns with all their vertical arrows, and leave every other column unchanged. Thus the results are the same full diagram $E$. Step 3 ensures both further reductions are admissible, even if an intermediate or final composite is entirely identities.

source.place: Definition 2.1, printed p.19, operations (iv)′ and (v)′; explicit elementary verification of their local overlaps, written by Q02, for Proposition 5.5, printed p.24

proof.text: These cases exhaust the two operations: two deletions have equal or disjoint singleton supports; a deletion and a composition have disjoint supports or the singleton lies in the pair; two compositions have equal pairs, disjoint pairs, or share exactly one column, the triple case. In the equal-result cases steps 4 and 6 give $D_1=D_2$. Otherwise steps 5 and 7 construct $E$ with exactly one further reduction from each branch. All comparisons included the signs, vertex objects and both kinds of arrows. This proves the stated strong diamond property.
